title: Value-Based Care Revenue Cycle Implications Playbook (CleanClaimRx Operational Playbook Series)
audience: Independent practices in Medicare Advantage risk contracts, MSSP ACOs, PCMH programs or MIPS reporting; written to billing and revenue cycle teams, practice administrators and owners. Examples run from a solo practice to a 40-clinician group, with office-based primary care as the main target.
summary: Argues that value-based payments are a second revenue stream that a fee-for-service billing operation never sees, and that the revenue cycle team should own it. Surveys MIPS, MSSP ACOs, ACO REACH, Medicare Advantage risk contracts and PCMH, then explains MIPS scoring and its two-year payment lag, the end of the 5% APM bonus, ACO benchmarks and attribution, HCC risk adjustment under the V28 model, PCMH per-member fees and quality-measure documentation. Central method: inventory which programs apply, measure current standing (MIPS score, chronic-condition recapture, wellness-visit completion, ACO quality), close the largest gaps, then run a monthly value-based report with separate financial-statement lines. Includes a self-assessment, a 90-day plan, a deadline calendar and two checklists. Rules are keyed to calendar year 2026. Dollar examples are uncited and in places contradict each other, and several MIPS details are outdated or wrong.

outline.gist: States rules reflect the 2026 physician fee schedule final rule and fully phased-in V28; examples are illustrative; not legal or coding advice.
Clean claims do not protect MIPS scores, risk scores or ACO quality; sizes the stakes with MIPS, risk-adjustment and shared-savings examples.
Compares MIPS, MSSP, ACO REACH, Medicare Advantage risk and PCMH by risk, payment mechanism and eligibility; three questions to ask before joining.

outline.section: Section 2: MIPS and APM Payment Adjustments
outline.gist: Two-year lag, 75-point threshold, budget-neutral bonuses, category weights, small-practice reweighting, MVPs, and qualifying-participant status after the 5% bonus ended.
Benchmarks, claims-based assignment, APP Plus measures, BASIC versus ENHANCED tracks, prepaid savings, and why the ACO's own distribution formula matters.

outline.section: Section 4: HCC Coding and Risk Adjustment
outline.gist: Risk scores drive capitation; V24-to-V28 changes; documentation-support standard; yearly recapture via wellness visits; dollar example; audit and False Claims Act exposure.

outline.section: Section 5: PCMH Qualification and Quality Bonus Revenue
outline.gist: NCQA's six concept areas, per-member monthly fees of roughly $2 to $15, layered quality bonuses, and tracking these payments separately.
Claims-based versus EHR-extracted measures, structured data entry, and the wellness visit as the one encounter feeding several programs.

outline.section: Section 7: The Data Infrastructure Value-Based Contracts Require
outline.gist: Three data sources (claims, EHR, payer feeds), CCLF files, template configuration, monthly reporting, QPP portal checks, diagnosing the need before buying tools.

outline.section: Section 8: Avoiding Common Value-Based Payment Errors
outline.gist: Lists typical omission and commission errors for MIPS, HCC capture, ACO attribution and PCMH; the common fix offered is in-year monitoring.
Monthly value-based report, ownership roles, separate financial-statement lines, clinician engagement, HCC audit, contract reading, absolute versus relative benchmarks, specialty notes.

outline.section: Section 10: Your Value-Based Revenue Opportunity Assessment
outline.gist: Yes/no self-assessment for MIPS, HCC, ACO and PCMH; rule-of-thumb gap estimate; asserts opportunity equals 5% to 15% of Medicare revenue.
Month 1 measure, month 2 close gaps, month 3 build recurring reporting; then quarterly reviews, semi-annual audit sample and an annual deadline calendar.
Checkboxes for eligibility and setup, quality, promoting interoperability, improvement activities and year-end submission and review.
Checkboxes for per-patient annual capture, documentation support, V28 code checks, population tracking and audit readiness; several items duplicated.

outline.section: Closing: The Revenue Cycle That Sees Both Streams
outline.gist: Rhetorical recap: value-based leakage is silent, so build measurement; cross-sells other catalog titles; no new content.

outline.section: Important Notes on This Playbook (back-matter disclaimer)
outline.gist: Says benchmark figures are commonly cited ranges and vendor-observed patterns are experience, not studies; confirm rules before acting.

ACO and risk-contract agreement review (minimum savings rate, sharing rate, distribution formula)

processes.name: Monthly value-based revenue report
steps: Estimate the current MIPS composite score and compare it with 75 points
Calculate the share of Medicare Advantage patients with all chronic conditions recaptured this year
Calculate Annual Wellness Visit completion for eligible Medicare patients
Pull ACO quality standing on APP Plus measures from the ACO
List submission, exception, registration and payer reporting deadlines falling within 90 days
Review with the owner and assign gap-closing actions
processes.owner_role: Practice administrator or office manager in small practices; dedicated value-based coordinator in larger ones

processes.name: Annual MIPS cycle
steps: Verify each clinician's eligibility and special statuses on the QPP site, and re-verify mid-year
Choose the reporting pathway and register if using an MVP
Confirm category weights (small-practice reweighting if 15 or fewer clinicians)
Select six quality measures, including an outcome or high-priority measure, where the practice can beat benchmark
Track data completeness of at least 75% per measure during the year
Document improvement activities the practice actually performs
Meet Promoting Interoperability requirements or file the hardship exception by December 31
Submit data by March 31 of the following year
Review the final score and dispute errors
Run next year's measure selection in the fourth quarter using new benchmarks
processes.owner_role: Staff member designated as responsible for MIPS (not specified further)
processes.cadence: Annual, with a monthly portal login and quarterly checklist review

processes.name: Annual HCC recapture cycle
steps: Obtain current risk-score reports from each contracted Medicare Advantage plan
Screen the panel for chronic conditions not yet documented this calendar year
Schedule a wellness visit or other qualifying visit for those patients
Have the clinician address each active condition and document current clinical support
Code to the most specific diagnosis and confirm it appears on a claim
Re-screen in the fourth quarter and close remaining gaps before December 31
processes.owner_role: Billing and coding staff together with the treating clinician

processes.name: Two-way HCC documentation audit
steps: Sample encounters carrying chronic-condition diagnoses
Test each coded condition for current-visit documentation support and V28 specificity
Flag unsupported diagnoses for removal and missed conditions for capture
Quantify compliance risk and revenue opportunity separately
Feed findings into clinician education and template changes
Have a qualified coding professional perform or oversee the review
processes.owner_role: Coding auditor or qualified coding professional

processes.name: Annual Wellness Visit completion workflow
steps: Identify Medicare patients eligible for a wellness visit this year
Run outreach to those who have not had one
Schedule in person or by video
Use the visit to review the full problem list and quality-measure items
Bill correctly and confirm the claim
Track the completion rate monthly
processes.owner_role: Not specified (scheduling and outreach staff implied)
processes.cadence: Monthly tracking; outreach launched in month 2 of the plan

processes.name: ACO attribution and agreement review
steps: Confirm which risk track the ACO occupies and the practice's shared-loss exposure
Read the participation agreement for minimum savings rate, sharing rate and distribution formula
Confirm primary-care claims go out promptly under the identifiers registered with the ACO
Tell patients about voluntary alignment
Request the practice's own subset of the ACO's CCLF claims data
Compare ACO quality reports with thresholds
processes.cadence: At joining or renewal and annually; claim checks ongoing

processes.name: Value-based revenue opportunity assessment (Section 10)
steps: Work through the MIPS, HCC, ACO and PCMH yes/no questions with each program's owner
Estimate the HCC gap with the per-0.1-RAF rule of thumb
Combine the programs into a total opportunity figure
Tie the result to existing fee-for-service KPIs
processes.owner_role: Practice leadership with the staff responsible for each program

processes.name: 90-day implementation plan
steps: Month 1: pull MIPS trajectory, eligibility, measure rates, plan risk-score reports, recapture screen, ACO quality report and wellness-visit rate
Month 2: launch wellness-visit outreach, build the recapture workflow, fix weak MIPS measures, confirm the hardship deadline, submit delayed primary-care claims
Month 3: start the monthly report, extend the coding audit to HCC, confirm EHR structured fields, finish the assessment
Afterwards: quarterly program reviews, semi-annual HCC audit sample, annual full assessment

metrics.name: MIPS final score (estimated trajectory)
metrics.definition: Composite 0-100 score across Quality, Cost, Promoting Interoperability and Improvement Activities, estimated during the year and compared with the performance threshold
metrics.formula: Weighted sum of category scores: 30% Quality, 30% Cost, 25% Promoting Interoperability, 15% Improvement Activities (small practice with interoperability reweighted: 40/30/0/30)
metrics.red_flag: Below 75 (sliding-scale penalty); 18.75 or lower draws the full -9%
metrics.source_cited: CMS and the CY2026 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, named generally with no citation

metrics.name: MIPS quality data completeness
metrics.definition: Share of a measure's eligible encounters for which data are captured and reported
metrics.formula: Reported eligible encounters / all eligible encounters for the measure
metrics.target: 75% or more for every selected measure
metrics.red_flag: Below 75% (heavy scoring loss regardless of clinical performance)

metrics.name: MIPS payment adjustment
metrics.definition: Percentage change applied to Medicare Part B payments two years after the performance year
metrics.formula: Adjustment percentage x Part B payments in the payment year
metrics.target: 0% or better; realistic bonus put at about 1% to 2.3%

metrics.name: Quality measure performance versus benchmark
metrics.definition: Each selected measure's performance rate compared with the CMS benchmark for its reporting mechanism
metrics.target: Above the benchmark average for each selected measure
metrics.red_flag: Measures chosen only because they are already documented

metrics.name: HCC capture (recapture) rate
metrics.definition: Share of the Medicare Advantage panel whose active chronic conditions have all been documented and coded again in the current year (defined once as with current-year documentation support, once as coded on a claim at least once)
metrics.formula: Patients with all active chronic conditions recaptured this year / Medicare Advantage patients with chronic conditions
metrics.red_flag: Example only: a clinician running 40% below the practice's own benchmark

metrics.name: Average RAF score for the Medicare Advantage panel
metrics.definition: Mean risk adjustment factor of the practice's Medicare Advantage patients, taken from plan-supplied reports and tracked quarterly
metrics.target: Compare with a 'specialty benchmark' (no value given)
metrics.red_flag: Example only: average understated by 0.15 per patient

metrics.name: HCC revenue gap estimate
metrics.definition: Annual dollars forgone because risk scores understate patient complexity
metrics.formula: (RAF gap per patient / 0.1) x $400 to $800 x number of Medicare Advantage patients

metrics.name: Annual Wellness Visit completion rate
metrics.definition: Share of eligible Medicare patients who completed a wellness visit in the current year, tracked monthly
metrics.formula: Completed wellness visits / eligible Medicare patients
metrics.red_flag: Example treats 60% completion as a gap

metrics.name: ACO quality performance versus threshold
metrics.definition: Standing on the ACO's APP Plus quality measures relative to benchmark

metrics.name: Net collection rate including value-based payments
metrics.definition: The vendor's net collection rate KPI recalculated with value-based distributions added
metrics.formula: Add value-based distributions to both numerator and denominator of net collection rate

metrics.name: Value-based revenue opportunity as a share of Medicare revenue
metrics.definition: Estimated value-based dollars available relative to combined Medicare and Medicare Advantage revenue
metrics.formula: 5% to 15% x combined Medicare and Medicare Advantage revenue

metrics.name: PMPM care-management revenue
metrics.definition: Per-member-per-month fee revenue from payers that reward PCMH recognition
metrics.formula: Attributed members x PMPM rate x 12
metrics.red_flag: Buried in 'other income' instead of a dedicated line

metrics.name: Clean claim rate
metrics.target: 97% (used only as an illustration of fee-for-service excellence)

numeric_claims.claim: A practice with a 97% clean claim rate can still forgo 5% to 15% of total Medicare and Medicare Advantage revenue
MIPS adjustments run from a -9% penalty to a budget-neutral scaled bonus and apply two years after the performance year
Maximum positive MIPS adjustment was +1.05% for the 2026 payment year (called the lowest ever), +2.15% for 2025, +8.25% for 2024 and +2.34% for 2023
CMS projects for the 2028 payment year a median positive adjustment near 1.30% and a median negative adjustment near -1.88%
Performance threshold is 75 points, held through the 2028 performance year; the full -9% applies at 18.75 points or lower
Category weights are Quality 30%, Cost 30%, Promoting Interoperability 25%, Improvement Activities 15%
Practices with fewer than 16 clinicians are reweighted to Quality 40%, Cost 30%, Improvement Activities 30%, Promoting Interoperability 0%
Data completeness must reach at least 75% for each quality measure
CMS finalized 27 MVPs for 2026, six of them new (diagnostic radiology, interventional radiology, neuropsychology, pathology, podiatry, vascular surgery)
APM incentive payment was 5% through the 2024 payment year, 3.5% for 2025, 1.88% for 2026, and nothing afterwards
From 2026 qualifying participants get a 0.75% annual conversion-factor update versus 0.25% for others; the 2026 factors are $33.5675 and $33.4009, up 3.77% and 3.26% from $32.3465
Forty clinicians at $200,000 each ($8,000,000 of Part B) face a MIPS swing of about $804,000 to $907,200; a solo practice at $150,000 risks $13,500
$500,000 of Part B billing implies a $50,250 to $56,700 swing; $2,000,000 implies $201,000 to $226,800; an $800,000 surgical practice $80,400 to $90,720
MSSP has 476 ACOs, more than 650,000 providers and 11.2 million beneficiaries
ACO REACH High Needs minimum beneficiary threshold rose from 1,000 to 1,250 for the 2026 performance year
New MSSP agreements starting January 1, 2027 allow at most five years in an upside-only track
ACOs report under the APP Plus measure set from performance year 2025; the health equity adjustment was removed from 2026 quality scoring
CMS introduced a prepaid shared savings option starting with performance year 2025
V24 had 86 HCC categories and 9,797 mapped diagnosis codes; V28 has 115 categories and 7,770 codes (net -2,027)
V28 lowers average risk scores by 3.12% relative to V24
RADV audits resumed under a January 27, 2026 HPMS memo covering payment years 2018 to 2024
numeric_claims.source_cited: HPMS memo named by date only

numeric_claims.claim: The Department of Justice announced a $117.7 million False Claims Act settlement with Aetna/CVS Health in March 2026 over an add-only chart review program
numeric_claims.source_cited: Department of Justice (no link or case reference)

numeric_claims.claim: With 400 Medicare Advantage patients at a $900 base rate, RAF 1.20 pays about $1,080 a month versus $810 at 0.90 ($3,240 a year); a 0.15 average gap costs $65,000 to $130,000 a year
A practice with 500 Medicare Advantage patients whose RAF is understated by 0.15 forgoes $75,000 to $125,000 a year
The vendor has observed annual risk-adjustment gaps of roughly $50,000 to $200,000 in independent practices with modest Medicare Advantage panels
Each 0.1 of missed RAF is worth about $400 to $800 per patient per year
PCMH care-management fees run about $2 to $15 per member per month; 800 patients at $5 yields $48,000 a year
An Annual Wellness Visit yields about $180 in fee-for-service revenue; 300 visits (60% of 500 eligible) yield about $54,000
A physician 40% below benchmark on diabetic nephropathy capture can represent a $35,000 annual capitation difference
Value-based opportunity is typically 5% to 15% of Medicare plus Medicare Advantage revenue; $1,500,000 of such revenue implies $75,000 to $225,000

checkable_claims.claim: Small practices - fewer than 16 clinicians in the practice's MIPS-eligible group - receive automatic reweighting ... Promoting Interoperability drops to 0%, ... Quality rises to 40% and Improvement Activities to 30%, keeping Cost at 30%.
checkable_claims.section: Section 2: MIPS and APM Payment Adjustments
checkable_claims.why: Sets how a two-clinician practice's score is built (quality 40%, activities 30%). If the conditions are misstated (for example, submitting interoperability data cancels the reweighting), category planning and the final score are wrong.

checkable_claims.claim: CMS has finalized 75 points as the MIPS performance threshold and will maintain it through the 2028 performance year ... Below 75, the payment adjustment scales down linearly, reaching the full -9% cap at scores of 18.75 points or lower.
checkable_claims.section: Section 2: MIPS and APM Payment Adjustments
checkable_claims.why: Defines the penalty line and the full 9% cut. A wrong threshold or scale misprices the practice's largest value-based downside, on the order of $50,000 a year at its Medicare volume.

checkable_claims.claim: there is no lump-sum APM bonus for the 2025 performance year or later under current law ... For CY2026, this produced a final conversion factor of $33.5675 for QPs ... versus $33.4009 for non-QPs
checkable_claims.section: Section 2: MIPS and APM Payment Adjustments (APM Exception box)
checkable_claims.why: Bonus status and the conversion-factor differential drive the value of joining an Advanced APM and anchor Medicare revenue budgeting; the 'current law' statement may have been overtaken by 2026 legislation.

checkable_claims.claim: MVP registration must be completed before the performance year begins - a practice cannot retroactively elect an MVP pathway partway through the year.
checkable_claims.section: Section 2: MIPS Value Pathways; repeated in Checklist 1
checkable_claims.why: If registration actually runs during the performance year, as I believe, a practice following this would wrongly think an MVP is closed to it or would miss the real window.

checkable_claims.claim: Improvement Activities 15% - Attestation-based; at least one high-weighted or two medium-weighted activities the practice is actually performing.
checkable_claims.section: Section 2: The Four Performance Categories; repeated in Checklist 1
checkable_claims.why: Improvement activities are 30% of a reweighted small practice's score. I believe activity weighting was abolished from 2025; attesting to the wrong number or type of activities risks the category or wastes effort.

checkable_claims.claim: Maximum positive adjustment actually paid: +1.05% for the 2026 payment year (the lowest in the program's history); 2025 payment year +2.15%; 2023 payment year +2.34%; and an anomalous spike to +8.25% for the 2024 payment year.
checkable_claims.why: These figures carry the document's whole MIPS economic argument and every 'realistic swing' example; if invented or misremembered, the upside sizing is unreliable.

checkable_claims.claim: A practice still coding to V24-era habits - documenting 'chronic kidney disease' without a stage, or 'diabetes' without a documented complication - is systematically under-capturing RAF for its MA panel
checkable_claims.why: This is the document's core coding advice. I believe V28 pays the same for diabetes with or without complications, so training built on it chases documentation that changes nothing and invites upcoding pressure.

checkable_claims.claim: CMS resumed Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV) audit activity under a January 27, 2026 HPMS memo, covering payment years 2018 through 2024 ... unsupported diagnoses are recouped, sometimes with extrapolated penalties across the broader patient population.
checkable_claims.why: Describes the audit exposure behind all the compliance advice. The memo date is unverified and I recall a court vacating the extrapolation rule in 2025; wrong facts here misstate legal risk.

adopt.idea: Run MIPS as a penalty-avoidance program: size the exposure as up to 9% of Medicare Part B payments two years out, aim for at least the performance threshold, and budget any bonus at 1% to 2%.
adopt.why: The downside is several times the realistic upside, so effort belongs on securing threshold points, not on chasing a top score.
adopt.note: With roughly 55% Medicare fee-for-service on $1.0-1.1 million, a full penalty would be on the order of $50,000 a year. Confirm eligibility, small-practice status and reporting options on the QPP site first.

adopt.idea: Add a monthly value-based scorecard beside the fee-for-service dashboard: estimated MIPS score, wellness-visit completion, chronic-condition recapture, payer or ACO quality standing, and deadlines due within 90 days.
adopt.why: These revenues fail silently (no denial, no aging bucket), and by year-end the reporting windows have closed.
adopt.note: Fits an AI-agent billing operation well. The document supplies only five headings, so the layout, data sources and a mid-year MIPS score estimator have to be built.

adopt.idea: Give non-claim and adjustment revenue its own lines in the books: MIPS adjustments, shared savings, capitation or per-member fees, payer quality bonuses.
adopt.why: Lumped into 'other income', no one can tell which program earns its keep; a CFO needs program-level visibility.
adopt.note: Extend to medical-director stipends and any Medicare Advantage incentive payments. MIPS adjustments arrive inside claim payments, so posting rules must tag them from remittance codes; the document does not explain how.

adopt.idea: Reassess every chronic condition at least once a year, anchored on the wellness or comprehensive visit, document current clinical support, and code to the most specific diagnosis.
adopt.why: Risk scores are rebuilt each year from that year's encounters; conditions not addressed and coded drop out.
adopt.note: The practice appears to be paid fee-for-service by its Medicare Advantage plans, so the capitation math does not reach it directly. Value comes through plan incentive programs, any future ACO or institutional special-needs-plan arrangement, and accurate records. Never code for payment alone.

adopt.idea: Make chart review two-way: every review looks for unsupported diagnoses to remove as well as missed ones to add, with a qualified coder overseeing.
adopt.why: One-way, add-only reviews are the pattern federal enforcers have pursued under the False Claims Act.
adopt.note: Write it into AI-agent governance as a hard rule: any agent that proposes diagnoses must also flag unsupported ones, with human sign-off.

adopt.idea: Fold diagnosis-support review into the existing coding audit: sample encounters, test each coded chronic condition for documentation support and specificity, and report compliance risk and missed capture separately.
adopt.why: One audit program yields both outputs and avoids a separate initiative.
adopt.note: The document suggests a semi-annual sample but gives no sample size or scoring rubric.

adopt.idea: Before joining or renewing any ACO, risk or incentive contract, read the agreement itself for attribution rules, minimum savings rate, sharing rate, downside exposure, distribution formula, and whether benchmarks are absolute or relative.
adopt.why: The distribution formula, not practice performance alone, decides what is paid; relative benchmarks can cut payment even while performance improves.
adopt.note: Directly useful for evaluating ACO offers and Medicare Advantage amendments, and a ready due-diligence checklist for a consulting service.

adopt.idea: Protect attribution with billing hygiene: bill primary-care services promptly under the correct participating tax ID and clinician, and tell patients about voluntary alignment.
adopt.why: Attribution is driven by claims; billing gaps can assign a patient the practice treats to someone else.
adopt.note: A facility-based practice needs the program-specific rules on which visit codes and places of service count toward assignment; the document does not cover them.

adopt.idea: Before buying any analytics or reporting product, decide whether the problem is missing data, a workflow that does not act on data, or lack of visibility.
adopt.why: A dashboard cannot fix information that was never captured in usable form.
adopt.note: A sound general rule for the practice's own technology spending and for advising other practices.

adopt.idea: Calendar the value-based year: verify eligibility and special statuses at least twice a year, choose measures in the fourth quarter against new benchmarks, and track submission and exception deadlines.
adopt.why: Eligibility and benchmarks change annually, and missed windows cannot be reopened.
adopt.note: Check every date against the QPP site; the document's statement on MVP registration timing looks wrong.

practice_relevance.why: MIPS almost certainly applies to a two-clinician practice with about 55% Medicare fee-for-service, and the penalty exposure is material, so Section 2 and the MIPS checklist matter. But the small-practice specifics this practice would actually use (claims-based quality codes, small-practice bonus and scoring floors, hospital-based or facility-based special statuses, geriatric measure choices) are thin or wrong. The Medicare Advantage capitation and PCMH material assumes an office-based primary-care panel under delegated risk; this practice is facility-based and, as far as the context shows, paid fee-for-service by its plans. Nothing addresses nursing-facility attribution, institutional special needs plans, the institutional risk model, Medicaid managed care, dual-eligibles, VA or Tricare. Its value is as a conceptual map, for the CFO view (separate revenue lines, contract reading, two-year MIPS lag), and as a module outline for a consulting service.
sections_that_do_not_apply: Section 5: PCMH Qualification and Quality Bonus Revenue (no office-based panel or PCMH recognition)
Section 4 capitation worked examples (assume delegated risk or percent-of-premium contracts)
Section 3 shared-savings mechanics (apply only if the practice joins an ACO)
Six new specialty MVPs in Section 2
Section 9 notes for surgical, behavioral health and rural practices

accuracy_concerns: MVP registration: the document says it must be completed before the performance year starts. As I understand QPP rules, registration opens around April 1 and closes around November 30 of the performance year itself. The error appears twice (Section 2 and Checklist 1).

Improvement activities: 'one high-weighted or two medium-weighted' reflects rules that ended after 2024. Weighting was removed for 2025 onward (two activities, or one for small, rural or non-patient-facing practices and MVP reporters).

Quality scoring: says topped-out or high-priority measures can earn an extra bonus point. Those bonuses ended after the 2021 performance year, and topped-out measures are generally capped at 7 points, the opposite of a bonus.

The claim that eCQMs get 'flat benchmarks' for their first two years does not match MIPS scoring as I know it; it looks like a conflation of new-measure scoring floors with the flat benchmarks used for certain measures in the ACO pathway.

Claims-based quality reporting is described as derived from codes already on the claim. In MIPS, Part B claims reporting requires adding quality data codes to each eligible claim and is open only to small practices; neither point is stated.

MSSP participation and assignment are described at the NPI level ('NPI not registered with the ACO'). MSSP works at the tax-ID level; the real failure mode is billing under a non-participant TIN. Voluntary alignment is a beneficiary option program-wide, not something 'some ACOs use'.
Prepaid shared savings is dated to performance year 2025; as I recall the option was finalized in the 2025 rule with first payments from January 1, 2026.
QP status is said to bring 'use of the simplified APM Performance Pathway'. That pathway is a MIPS reporting option for APM participants who are not exempt, so the sentence is confused.

Medicare Advantage risk adjustment is presented as a same-year effect. The model is prospective: diagnoses from one calendar year set payment for the next. The cash-timing point a revenue-cycle guide should teach is missing.

The V28 example uses V24 logic. Under V28, diabetes with and without complications carries the same weight, so 'diabetes without a documented complication' is not an under-capture of the diabetes category (kidney-disease staging does matter). The $35,000 'diabetic nephropathy' example inherits the flaw.

MEAT is presented as the standard CMS audits apply. It is an industry convention (usually Monitor, Evaluate, Assess, Treat), not a CMS-defined rule; auditors apply coding guidelines and medical-record requirements.

RADV: the 'January 27, 2026 HPMS memo' is unverified, and extrapolation is described as live with no mention that a federal district court vacated the 2023 RADV rule in September 2025 (as I recall). RADV audits target plans; practices feel them through record requests and contract terms.

'2024 expansion of definitive drug testing into HCC mapping' is not a real policy as far as I know; drug-testing laboratory codes have nothing to do with diagnosis-based risk categories. Treat as fabricated.
The statement that remission-status mental health diagnoses lost HCC credit is overgeneralized; it holds for major depression in remission but not across all psychiatric conditions.

Capitation dollars are presented as practice revenue. Most independent practices paid fee-for-service by Medicare Advantage plans receive none of the plan's risk-adjusted premium unless a risk or incentive contract says so; the document never draws this line.

A wellness visit is valued at about $180. National Medicare rates for the far more common subsequent wellness visit are well below that unless add-on services are assumed; verify against the local fee schedule.
Says a neutral MIPS adjustment 'costs nothing' beyond timely, complete reporting. Reaching 75 points takes measured performance; many small and solo practices have been penalized despite reporting.
Recalculating net collection rate with value-based payments in numerator and denominator is methodologically unsound: it blends non-claim revenue into a claim-level diagnostic and inflates it.
Maximum positive adjustment for the 2024 payment year is given as 8.25% (CMS reported 8.26% as I recall); the 1.05% figure for 2026 and the 'CMS projection' medians carry no source.

'No lump-sum APM bonus under current law' may be wrong as of the September 2026 generation date; I recall the February 2026 appropriations law restoring a reduced bonus for the 2026 performance year. Verify.
The Closing's claim that better HCC capture raises next year's benchmark and earnings ignores MSSP caps on risk-score growth and Medicare Advantage normalization and coding-intensity adjustments.
The ACO REACH High Needs threshold change (1,000 to 1,250) is unverified.
internal_contradictions: Risk-adjustment dollar conversions disagree by roughly four to ten times: Introduction (500 patients, 0.15 gap = $75,000-$125,000); Section 4 (400 patients, 0.15 gap, $900 base = $65,000-$130,000, although its own arithmetic gives about $648,000); Section 10 ($400-$800 per 0.1 RAF per patient, which is $240,000-$480,000 for 400 patients).

Section 2 says the top bonus ran far below 9% in every recent payment year, then lists 8.25% for the 2024 payment year in the same sentence; the 'realistic range' used in every worked example silently drops that year.

Says small practices get automatic Promoting Interoperability reweighting, yet the plan and checklist tell the practice to file a hardship exception and to submit the e-prescribing measure, without warning that submitting data cancels the automatic reweighting.
Timing of risk-score effects: Section 4 implies a same-year payment impact; the Closing says improved capture pays off next year.
HCC capture rate is defined two ways: documented with current-year support (Section 9) versus merely coded on a claim once in the year (Checklist 2).

Cross-references overpromise: Section 3 says Section 9 covers how to read the ACO agreement, and Section 2 points to Section 7 for real-time MIPS monitoring; each gets one short paragraph and no method.
Front matter calls the worked-example dollars illustrative, while the body presents the same ranges as what the vendor 'has observed' in practices.
time_sensitive_or_outdated: All MIPS and fee-schedule content is keyed to the 2026 rule. The 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule is normally published around the start of November 2026 and supersedes thresholds, weights, measure lists and conversion factors for 2027 planning; not reflected.
Improvement-activity weighting (ended after 2024) and quality bonus points (ended after 2021) are stale rules presented as current.
MSSP size figures (476 ACOs, 11.2 million beneficiaries) match CMS's January 2025 release; 2026 participation figures were available well before September 2026.
ACO REACH is described as a live alternative with no mention that 2026 is its final performance year or of the successor model CMS announced for 2027 (verify).
'No APM bonus under current law' and the unstated QP thresholds depend on legislation that changed in early 2026 (verify).
RADV status is moving (2023 rule vacated in 2025, appeals and CMS audit plans in flux); any statement about years covered or extrapolation needs a current check.

No mention of the 2027 Medicare Advantage payment policy published in April 2026, which as I recall limits risk-score credit for diagnoses sourced only from chart reviews not linked to an encounter; directly relevant to the retrospective-review advice (verify).
Telehealth wellness-visit advice depends on Medicare telehealth flexibilities that carry statutory end dates; the document gives none.
'2015 Edition Cures Update' is superseded certification terminology.
The maximum-adjustment history stops at the 2026 payment year; results for the 2027 payment year (2025 performance) were likely available by late summer 2026.
ai_generation_signals: Leftover editing artifacts: a boxed heading that begins 'CORRECTED:' and a bullet promising mechanics 'corrected against' historical outcomes, traces of a revision pass rather than finished copy.
Self-referential phrasing ('described in this playbook as...', 'repeatedly described throughout this playbook').
First-hand experience claims ('CCRx has observed', 'in CCRx's experience') from a vendor with no named author, credential or data.
A HIPAA breach-log deadline dropped into the value-based deadline calendar, apparently carried over from another title.
A fabricated-sounding rule (definitive drug testing 'into HCC mapping') and a contentless aside on Stark Law for behavioral health.
Checklist 2 repeats the same V28 code-list and add-and-remove items in two separate blocks.
Slogan repetition ('Same discipline. Different revenue stream.'), the wellness visit declared the top-leverage encounter three times, and a two-page closing with no new content.
Cross-sell references to other catalog titles in place of substance (Coding Audit Playbook, KPI Prescription 08, Annual Assessment Guide Domain 8, Telehealth playbook).
Tidy round-number worked examples and precise-looking statistics with no citations anywhere in 40 pages.
Awkward machine phrasing ('a performance threshold that resets confusion every reporting cycle').
missing_for_real_use: Low-volume threshold values and the opt-in option are never stated, so a reader cannot tell whether MIPS applies.

No measure IDs, quality data codes or collection-type guidance; nothing on small-practice specifics (claims reporting, quality bonus points, scoring floors) or on hospital-based and facility-based special statuses.
No mid-year MIPS score estimator or worksheet, although in-year monitoring is the stated fix for every error.
No layout, data dictionary or sample for the monthly report; no template behind any checklist item.
No explanation of how MIPS adjustments appear on remittances (adjustment and remark codes) or how to post them to a separate line.
No targeted-review (score dispute) window or steps.

No account of how a practice is actually paid for risk-adjustment work: percent-of-premium, gainshare, per-gap or per-assessment incentives, plan Stars and HEDIS bonus programs; no contract-term checklist.

No risk-adjustment mechanics a coder needs: acceptable provider and visit types, face-to-face rule, audio-only exclusion, model segments (community, institutional, dual status), payment-year timing and submission deadlines.

No compliance guardrails beyond add-and-delete: no high-risk diagnosis list (history-of versus active cancer, acute stroke or heart attack coded in follow-up care), no clinician query process, no overpayment-refund duty, no policy on diagnoses arising only from wellness visits or health risk assessments.
Nothing for facility-based care: nursing-facility and assisted-living attribution rules, institutional special needs plans, long-term-institutional risk scores, high-needs ACO models.
Nothing on Medicaid managed care value-based programs, dual-eligibles, VA, Tricare or commercial programs.

No link to care-management billing (chronic care management, transitional care, advanced primary care management, advance care planning), the fee-for-service codes most tied to value-based performance.
No cost side: registry or vendor fees, staff hours, clinician time; no return-on-investment test per program.
No ACO selection due diligence (track record, fees, data access, exclusivity, exit terms).
No citations, links or rule references for any number; no author or reviewer credential.
